newsitem.title: UK: UK's Clarke says not sure EMU will start in 1999.
newsitem.headline: UK's Clarke says not sure EMU will start in 1999.

text.p: UK Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke said he believed European Monetary Union would go ahead but was not sure about the proposed January 1, 1999 start date.
"I think the probability is it will happen.," he told BBC Radio. "I'm not so sure about January 1, 1999 but it will be somewhere around, I think, the end of the century."

"I strongly hold to the view that the British as key players in this market have got to play a part in all this and keep the option ready to exercise it, one way or the other, whenever the decision is taken to go ahead," Clarke added.
Asked if he shared concerns that the City of London could suffer if Britain stayed out of the single currency, he replied:
"This is one reason for doing the negotiations -- it underlines the need to be there to make sure it isn't the case. We have to be ready whether or not we join."
Clarke said some recent reporting about the possible risks to London had been "off the wall."

"But behind that lay a lot of details whereby the City of London could certainly be threatened -- industry could be threatened -- if we stayed outside the single currency and the arrangements that were entered into were not ones that were right for us inside the market," he added.
Clarke said he agreed with chief executives and chairmen from 15 top companies, who wrote a letter to Thursday's Financial Times warning about the risks of Britain opting-out.

"It coincides with what the prime minister has said, with what I've said, that it's absolutely crucial we keep our role, we negotiate, we take part in order to make sure that when we exercise our option, the planning of all the detail on this is of a kind which the British would approve of."
